posts.caption:
How to stop filing paper and find any document in two seconds using only your phone's camera.

No new app. No scanner. No system to keep up with. Photograph it, name it, search it.

Save this for the next pile on the kitchen counter.
posts.caption_fb:
There's a drawer in most houses that everybody's scared of. Receipts, guarantees, school letters, that one form you're sure you kept. I used to have one too.

Here's the whole fix: photograph it. Phone flat over the page, good light, one photo per page. Then swipe up on the photo and type what it is — "car service June". That's it. Later you type "service" into Photos and it hands it back to you. Your phone can even read the words printed on the page, so it finds things you never even labelled.

You don't need a filing system. Paper doesn't need a home — it needs a copy. Do one pile tonight and tell me how it went.

posts.caption:
How to stop missing appointments without buying a planner or downloading another app — one shared calendar, one rule.

Four places to keep a date means no places. Pick one. Say it instead of typing it.

Which date is only in your head right now?
posts.caption_fb:
Most households I've sat in run on four systems at once. Sticky notes on the fridge, a diary next to the kettle, dates buried in a school WhatsApp group, and whatever's left in somebody's head. Then everyone's surprised when something gets missed.

It isn't a memory problem. Four places means no places.

One rule fixes it: if it has a date, it goes in the calendar. Use the calendar that's already on your phone, call it Home, and share it with whoever else needs to see it. Doctor, school, birthdays, the car licence, the plumber — all of it, no matter how small it feels. And don't type it. Hold the side button and say "add dentist Tuesday at three to Home". Twelve seconds, hands still on the wheel.

The fridge can keep the drawings. Nobody has to carry the dates anymore.

posts.caption:
Why capable people feel slow and behind — it isn't discipline, it's the hidden admin of modern life.

We built the tools to save time, then inherited the job of managing them. Infinite tools, finite bandwidth.

One question tonight: how much of your day goes on using tools, and how much goes on managing them?
posts.caption_fb:
I want to name something, because I don't think most people have words for it.

Think about what you actually did today. Chased a password. Approved an update you didn't ask for. Hunted for the right app. Cleared notifications. Looked for a document you knew you had. None of that was the work. All of it took the day.

We built these tools for convenience, and somewhere along the line we inherited a second job managing them — the accounts, the updates, the twelve places one thing could live. Infinite tools, finite bandwidth. That's the Modern Paradox, and it's arithmetic, not a character flaw.

It's why people who are genuinely good at what they do feel slow. They haven't lost anything. They're just working a shift nobody ever named.

Don't fix anything tonight. Just ask yourself the question: how much of my day goes on using tools, and how much goes on managing them? Sit with the answer. We'll deal with the fix another day.
